newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Grieving Thredbo sick of the glare of world media.
newsitem.headline: Grieving Thredbo sick of the glare of world media.

text.p: The alpine villagers of Thredbo, well used to the blinding glare of snow and ice, are not coping with being in the sometimes brutal spotlight of the world's media.

Since a landslide tore through this Australian ski village last Wednesday night, destroying two lodges and burying 19 people beneath tonnes of rubble, hundreds of reporters have invaded the tiny, grief-stricken community.
And they have not been entirely welcome.

The villagers, virtually all of whom have a friend or know of someone feared dead in the disaster, accuse news media of being "pushy" and insensitive in their excitement to report the extraordinary events of the past six days.
Reporters, photographers and television camera crews have told of being abused in the village's few local restaurants and bars, where emotional villagers and journalists have rubbed shoulders.

One villager is said to have tipped a glass of beer on a television journalist and the Thredbo petrol station taped a notice to its door saying, "Media are NOT welcome here." A footnote said the local radio station's reporter was exempted.
"I know they've got a job to do but they've gone too far," said a woman working for a hotel-booking and information office.
"They want to extend their stay but our priority is the emergency workers involved in the rescue."
New South Wales state politician Peter Cochran, who represents the area, said members of the media at Thredbo disobeyed police instructions and bugged police transmissions.
Cochran said, quoting police, that a drunken female journalist abused rescue workers for not taking more action.

"There are some elements within the media which have inaccurately reported events of the past few days and brought great distress and suffering to relatives and behaved quite improperly around the site," Cochran said in a radio interview.
Cochran offered no proof of the charges.
Acting prime minister Tim Fischer, who regularly hikes through the Snowy Mountains, has also expressed concern and said he wants the Press Council to investigate the media's behaviour.
But rescuers have supported the media, especially the coverage of the miraculous survival of ski instructor Stuart Diver who was unearthed from a concrete tomb on Saturday night.
Only two days ago, police spokesman Kevin Daley paid tribute to the media, saying: "Thank you very much. You have been an excellent, disciplined group."

A religious leader praised the media during a church service in Thredbo on Monday, saying the coverage of the disaster had united Australia behind the tiny village which boasts a permanent population of barely 500.

"I know that the media hasn't been without criticism during these days, but they have done a great service to Australia in helping all of us be aware of the plight (that) you people here in Thredbo have suffered," said Catholic Bishop Patrick Power.

Chris Warren, federal secretary of the journalists' union, the Media, Entertainment & Arts Alliance, said allegations of improper behaviour of reporters covering the landslide should not overshadow the overall sensitive handling of the tragedy.
"It's inevitable that in this instance there will be some conflict and there will be some people who will do things in retrospect they wish they hadn't," Warren said.

The Bulletin news magazine's Kerry-Anne Walsh, who was asked to leave a restaurant after she identified herself as a journalist, said: "You are going to get a few bad apples who will give us a bad name, but by and large we have been a very responsible lot here".
"It's just such a small place. We are probably going one for one in terms of the media presence here and the local population."
